title: Advent: Mary's candle
hookLine: the fourth Sunday remembers Mary's yes

cards: An angel comes in to a young woman in Nazareth. Luke doesn't describe the room. He gives names instead: the angel is Gabriel, the young woman is Mary, and she is promised in marriage to a man called Joseph.
The greeting troubles her. What comes next sounds impossible: she will have a son, and his kingdom will have no end. She doesn't faint.
She doesn't simply nod. She asks a question. Then she gives an answer that is still repeated, and on the fourth Sunday of Advent, the last candle before Christmas, it comes back.

teach.h: HAIL, THE LORD IS WITH THEE.
teach.b: Gabriel's first words, in the King James Bible: "Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." Luke says plainly that "she was troubled at his saying".
Then comes the promise of a son, and Mary's reply is honest and practical: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" The angel doesn't scold her for asking.
He explains, as far as it can be explained, and ends: "For with God nothing shall be impossible."

teach.h: BE IT UNTO ME: LET IT BE.
teach.b: Then Mary answers: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." In the Latin Bible the word is fiat, let it be, and tradition calls this moment her fiat. Look at the shape of it.
Troubled. A real question. Then yes, with her eyes open.
It isn't a yes because nothing frightened her. It's a yes after the question, in a young woman's mouth, with everything riding on it.
Churches honor that yes differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians honor Mary as the Mother of God and ask her to pray for them; the Hail Mary begins with Gabriel's greeting.

Protestant churches, in their own ways, honor her as a model of trusting faith, and direct their prayers to God alone. Some churches call the fourth Advent candle Mary's candle; others name it for love, or for the angels.
Whatever the name, Luke's sentence from Nazareth stands near the end of the waiting.

how: On the fourth Sunday of Advent, churches that keep the season light the last candle on the wreath and often read Luke's account of the angel's visit to Mary; Catholics and Orthodox also pray the Hail Mary or other prayers that honor her.

s: in Luke, Mary says yes without asking anything
she asks first: "how shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
fiat, the Latin word for Mary's answer, means let it be
tradition calls her yes her fiat: be it unto me according to thy word.
every church names the fourth Advent candle for Mary

games.q: you're Mary. an angel has just told you that you will have a son whose kingdom will have no end. what do you say first?
o: nothing; you simply bow your head.
games.why: Luke 1:34. Mary asks an honest question first, and only then says: "be it unto me according to thy word."

practice: Find something good you've been holding at arm's length, a call you keep putting off, a kindness you could offer, and first ask your honest question: how, and what will it cost? Then, when you're ready, quietly say a small yes.
If you pray, you can pray Mary's words, be it unto me according to thy word; if you don't, simply say inside, let it be.

wordCard.voice: Advent. The weeks of waiting before Christmas. Its fourth Sunday, in some churches, remembers Mary's yes: be it unto me according to thy word.

orig.note: Greek: may it be — Mary's word in Luke 1:38. the Latin Bible renders it fiat.

carryVoice: Your line: let it be. A yes can come after a question. Same time tomorrow.
